# Issues

An issue is a promise that someone can pick this up without you. Everything
below exists to make that true.

**You write it yourself.** Not a subagent: what makes an issue worth reading is
the evidence — the command, its output, what was expected, what was already
tried — and all of it is in your context and nowhere else. Handing it over
means summarising it first, which is the one thing `kx-style` says never to do
to a trace.

**Where it goes:** this project's repository, from `git remote get-url origin`.
Never kx — a bug in kx itself is `kx report`, which files on kx and redacts the
trace first.

## Open one only for work that is not being done now

If it is being fixed in this session, fix it. An issue filed for something
closed twenty minutes later is noise in a list people have to read.

What is worth one: a defect nobody is fixing today, a gap found while doing
something else, a decision that needs someone who is not here.

Then two checks, in this order, before writing a word:

```bash
gh issue list --search "<the words the reporter would have used>" --state all
```

Found one → add what is new as a comment. Two issues for one defect split its
evidence, and the second gets closed as a duplicate without being read.

**And open the file.** An issue says a file says something, a command fails, a
version is wrong. Check it against the repository as it is now, not as it was
in the report. Already fixed → say so and file nothing; that is a triage round
somebody does not have to spend.

## The shape

```markdown
## Objective

<One sentence. What has to become true.>

## Done when

- [ ] <checkable by someone who was not here>
- [ ] <…>

## Evidence

<Verbatim: the command, its output, `file.ts:41`, the version, the platform.>

## Not in this

<What a reader would reasonably assume is included and is not.>
```

`## Context` last, and only when the reason is not obvious from the evidence.

**Objective** — a state of the world, not an activity. "`kx doctor` reports a
skipped check as passed" ends; "look into doctor" does not.

**Done when** — the test is whether a person who has never seen this issue
could tick a box without asking anybody. "Works properly", "is cleaner",
"handles errors" fail it. A command and its exit code, a file containing a
line, an output that no longer appears: those pass. Two or three boxes; ten is
a plan, and a plan belongs in the work.

**Evidence** — verbatim, never compressed, and never invented. Not reproduced
is written as `Not reproduced — seen once, on <what>`, which is a fact. A
guessed reproduction reads exactly like a real one and sends the next person
into the wrong file.

**Not in this** — one or two lines, and the cheapest part to write. It is what
stops the issue growing a second objective in its comments.

**The title** says what is wrong or what has to change, in the words the next
person will search for. Not the area: "auth" is a label, not a title. Under
~72 characters, no trailing period, and never a bare error message pasted in —
that is what a title looks like when a tool wrote it instead of a person.

## The rules

- **English, always** — including issues filed from a conversation in Spanish.
  Same reason as `kx-commit`: one language across the record keeps it
  greppable by whoever arrives later, tooling included.
- **One objective per issue.** Two things that could be finished on different
  days are two issues, filed separately. A bundle gets one label, one severity
  and one reading, and its smaller half is never done.
- **Never a credential.** An issue is public to everyone with repo access and
  cannot be unpublished. Traces hold whatever was on screen: name the
  variable, never the value.
- **No labels, no assignee, no milestone.** Labelling is triage, and the
  person writing an issue is a party to it. Nothing here knows who is free.
- **Never pad.** No "Steps to reproduce" heading with nothing under it, no
  summary restating the objective. An empty section reads as looked-at.
- **Show the person the exact body and ask.** Not a summary of it. Filing
  publishes it, and publishing is not something to do because a command ran.

Then, and only then:

```bash
gh issue create --repo <owner/repo> --title "<title>" --body-file <(cat <<'BODY'
<the body>
BODY
)
```

Print the URL. If `gh` refuses, say which of the three it is — not installed,
not signed in, or no access to that repository — and stop.
